---
title: "Look back and follow up"
description: >
  Fetch the records in a window of days around each person's entry: the 30 days
  after discharge, and the year before admission.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Keep the build machine out of printed query headers (load duckdb first, as it
# registers its own description when it loads).
loadNamespace("duckdb")
registerS3method("db_connection_describe", "duckdb_connection",
                 function(con, ...) "example database", envir = asNamespace("dbplyr"))
```

In [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html) you built `entries`: one
row per person, with the dates of their first admission for appendicitis. To
answer the running question, you now need two more sets of records for each
person:

- **Follow-up:** admissions for any cause in the 30 days after discharge, to
  find readmissions.
- **Look-back:** admissions in the year before the entry admission, where the
  next guide will look for diabetes.

Each person has their own dates, so each needs their own window. The picture
shows three people. Their windows sit at different dates, and a record comes
back only if it falls inside one of its own person's windows.

```{r windows-timeline, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Inline, so the diagram travels with the page and keeps its title and description.
cat("```{=html}", "<div style=\"margin: 0.5rem 0 1.5rem;\">",
    readLines("figures/windows-timeline.svg"), "</div>", "```", sep = "\n")
```

You fetch each kind of window with its own `thip_window()` call: follow-up
records into `followup`, look-back records into `history`.

Every example runs on the example database of invented records described in
[Meet the THIP data](meet-the-data.html); on THIP, connect with `thip_connect()`
instead.

## Rebuild the entries

This chunk repeats the code of [From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html)
in one go. It stacks the three yearly tables with converted dates, collects the
appendicitis records admitted in the study period (1 October 2021 to 31 August
2024), and keeps each person's first appendicitis admission with a valid
discharge date:

```{r entries}
library(thipR)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

con <- thip_connect_example()

admissions <- thip_table(
  con, tables = c("nhso2565", "nhso2566", "nhso2567"), .id = "source_table",
  dates = c(adm = "dateadm", dsc = "datedsc", death = "death_date"),
  date_format = c(adm = "%Y%m%d", dsc = "%Y%m%d", death = "%Y-%m-%d")
)

candidates <- admissions |>
  filter(adm >= as.Date("2021-10-01"), adm <= as.Date("2024-08-31")) |>
  thip_filter_icd(codes = "K35", cols = "pdx", match = "prefix") |>
  collect()

entries <- candidates |>
  filter(!is.na(dsc)) |>
  arrange(pid, adm, tran_id) |>
  distinct(pid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(pid, entry_id = tran_id, adm_date = adm, dsc_date = dsc)

entries
```

There are `r nrow(entries)` entries, one per person. `adm_date` and `dsc_date`
are `Date` values, which the windows below need.

## The round trip

`entries` is in R; the records are on the database. You cannot join the two the
usual way: thipR only reads from the database and never writes a table there,
and collecting whole yearly tables to join in R would be far too large. So
getting each person's records around their entry is a round trip:

1. `thip_window()` takes `entries` and makes a plan: for each entry, its `pid`
   and the first and last day of its window. Nothing is read yet.
2. `collect()` sends the plan to the database as a query. The database matches
   records to people by `pid`, checks each record's date against that person's
   window, and keeps only the records inside.
3. Those records come back to R as an ordinary data frame, with one extra
   column, `entry_id`, saying which entry each record belongs to.

The people and their dates travel inside the query itself, so nothing is
written to the database, and only the matching records are brought into R.

## A window is two day offsets

A window is set by a date on the entry, the **index**, and two whole numbers of
days counted from it, smallest first (the `L` marks a whole number in R;
`c(1, 31)` works too). Negative offsets count back before the index. For
readmission, the index is the discharge date:

- `window = c(1L, 31L)` sets the edges: day 1 and day 31 after discharge.
- `bounds = "[)"`, the default, says which edges count. `[` includes its edge
  and `)` excludes it.

So the follow-up window holds days 1 to 30 after discharge. A record admitted on
the day of discharge (day 0) is not in it, and nor is one admitted on day 31.
As long as an admission does not start after its own discharge, the entry
admission cannot be in its own follow-up window; you check this below.

The other three bounds move the edges:

| `bounds`         | `window = c(1L, 31L)` includes |
|------------------|--------------------------------|
| `"[)"` (default) | days 1 to 30                   |
| `"[]"`           | days 1 to 31                   |
| `"(]"`           | days 2 to 31                   |
| `"()"`           | days 2 to 30                   |

Offsets count days, not calendar months or years: `c(1L, 31L)` is always the
same 30 days, whatever the month.

## Plan the follow-up

The piped-in table is the records to search, `admissions`, trimmed to the
columns you need; `entries` is the second argument. `date = "adm"` names a
column of the records, the admission date, and `index = "dsc_date"` names a
column of `entries`:

```{r followup-plan}
followup_plan <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx) |>
  thip_window(entries, date = "adm", index = "dsc_date", window = c(1L, 31L))

followup_plan
```

Printing the plan reads no records: it describes `r nrow(entries)` entries for
`r nrow(entries)` people, waiting for `collect()`. In the printout, *source*
means the records you search (`admissions`) and *cohort* means `entries`. Do any
`select()` and `filter()` before `thip_window()`, as here; the plan is not a
table you can add more dplyr steps to.

Two arguments keep their defaults:

- `by = "pid"` names the person column. Here records and entries share the name;
  if your entries call it something else, map record column to entry column, as
  in `by = c(pid = "person")`. Both columns must hold the same kind of value:
  here, text.
- `entry = "entry_id"` names the column that identifies each entry. It must be
  unique, one value per row of `entries`, and must not also be a column of the
  records.

Both dates must be `Date` values, not text or date-times, which is why the plan
uses `adm` and `dsc_date`, not the text column `dateadm`. On the database, a
record date of the wrong type is caught when you `collect()`. Missing or blank
values in `entries` (person, entry, index, or start and end dates) stop
`thip_window()` with an error, one reason `entries` keeps only admissions with a
valid discharge date. A record with a missing `pid` or `adm` is never inside any
window, so check the date conversion before you rely on the result, as in
[From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html). `thip_window()` also works
on a local data frame of records, with the same rules.

## Collect the follow-up

`collect()` runs the plan and brings the matching records into R:

```{r followup}
followup <- collect(followup_plan)
glimpse(followup)
```

`followup` has the six selected columns plus `entry_id`, the last column, which
names the entry each record belongs to. The entries' own dates are not in it. To
check the window, join each entry's discharge date back, count the days from
discharge to each readmission, and check that no entry admission came back as
its own readmission:

```{r followup-days}
followup |>
  left_join(select(entries, entry_id, dsc_date), by = "entry_id") |>
  mutate(days_after = as.integer(adm - dsc_date)) |>
  count(days_after)

followup |>
  filter(tran_id == entry_id) |>
  nrow()
```

Every readmission starts between day 1 and day 30 after discharge, and none is
the entry admission itself.

## Count readmissions per entry

`followup` has rows only for entries that were readmitted. Person B in the
picture at the top is such an entry: it is in `entries` but has no rows in
`followup`. Each row will count as one readmission, so first check that no
record came back twice for the same entry; a record repeated in the source would
count as two readmissions:

```{r repeats}
followup |>
  count(entry_id, tran_id) |>
  filter(n > 1) |>
  nrow()
```

None did. If yours do, look at the repeated records and decide whether they are
the same admission before you count;
`distinct(entry_id, tran_id, .keep_all = TRUE)` keeps the first row of each,
with all its columns.

To count every entry, including those with no readmission, start from `entries`
and join the counts onto it:

```{r readmit}
readmit <- entries |>
  left_join(count(followup, entry_id, name = "readmissions"), by = "entry_id") |>
  mutate(readmissions = coalesce(readmissions, 0L),
         readmitted = readmissions > 0)

readmit |>
  summarise(entries = n(), readmitted = sum(readmitted)) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * readmitted / entries, 1))
```

`r sum(readmit$readmitted)` of the `r nrow(readmit)` entries were readmitted,
for any cause, within 30 days of discharge. To count only related readmissions,
filter `followup` on `pdx` first.

**Keep `entries` on the left.** Counting from `followup` alone, or with
`inner_join()`, drops the `r sum(!readmit$readmitted)` entries with no
readmission, and every entry left looks readmitted.

## Look back a year

The same function fetches the look-back records. Now the index is the admission
date, and the window ends at it:

```{r history}
history <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx, num_range("sdx", 1:20)) |>
  thip_window(entries, date = "adm", index = "adm_date", window = c(-365L, 0L)) |>
  collect()

ncol(history)
```

With `"[)"`, the window holds days −365 to −1: the 365 days before the entry
admission. The entry admission starts on day 0, so it is not in `history`; its
diagnoses are already in `candidates`. `history` keeps the principal diagnosis
and all 20 secondary diagnosis columns, which the next guide searches, plus
`entry_id`.

For a first look, count the history records of each entry, again starting from
`entries` so that entries with none are counted:

```{r history-count}
history_count <- entries |>
  left_join(count(history, entry_id, name = "history_records"), by = "entry_id") |>
  mutate(history_records = coalesce(history_records, 0L))

count(history_count, history_records, name = "entries")
```

Most entries have no admission found in the year before, in the tables you
stacked. No history records means none was found. That is not the same as
having no diabetes, and, as the next section shows, it does not always mean
that a whole year was searched. The split matches the readmission count by
chance: only
`r length(intersect(history$entry_id, followup$entry_id))` entry has both
history and a readmission.

## Windows and the years you stacked

A window does not stop at the end of a fiscal year: `admissions` stacks all
three yearly tables, so each window searches them all. It does stop at the edge
of what you stacked. Set those edges from the data, as in the span check in
[From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html): the first and last
admission dates in the stack. On THIP, take them from that check for the tables
you stacked, not from the tables' fiscal-year names:

```{r coverage}
span <- admissions |>
  summarise(first = min(adm, na.rm = TRUE), last = max(adm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  collect()
span

data_start <- span$first
data_end <- span$last

entries |>
  summarise(lookback_starts_early = sum(adm_date - 365L < data_start),
            followup_ends_late = sum(dsc_date + 30L > data_end))
```

In the example, admissions run from 1 October 2021 to 30 September 2024. For
`r sum(entries$adm_date - 365L < data_start)` entries the look-back starts
before the first admission date in the stack, so part of their year was never
searched: finding no history there can mean the records are in a table you did
not stack.

This is the look-back side of the room you left for follow-up in
[From question to cohort](question-to-cohort.html), where the study period stops
a month before the data end. There are two fixes. Stack the year before as well
(on THIP, add the previous year's table to `tables` and run the span check
again); the study period, and so `entries`, stay the same. Or start the study
period a year after the data begin, on 1 October 2022 in the example. The
example has no earlier table, so this course keeps all `r nrow(entries)`
entries, and the next guide reads a missing diabetes code as "not recorded in
the stacked years". The follow-up needs no fix: in the example, no follow-up
window runs past the last admission date in the stack.

## Explicit start and end dates

Instead of `index` and `window`, you can give each entry its own first and last
day, as two `Date` columns, with `start` and `end`. This is the same follow-up
window written as dates, with `"[]"` so that both days count:

```{r explicit}
followup_dates <- entries |>
  mutate(fu_start = dsc_date + 1L, fu_end = dsc_date + 30L)

followup_again <- admissions |>
  select(pid, tran_id, source_table, adm, dsc, pdx) |>
  thip_window(followup_dates, date = "adm", start = "fu_start", end = "fu_end",
              bounds = "[]") |>
  collect()

nrow(followup_again)
setequal(followup_again$tran_id, followup$tran_id)
```

The same records come back. Explicit dates are useful when a window is not a
fixed number of days from one date: from discharge to the end of the study, for
example, or to a date that differs from person to person. Give either `start`
and `end`, or `index` and `window`, not both.

## Batches and the window report

`collect()` sends people to the database in batches. `batch_size` is the most
people in one batch, 1,000 by default. It is not a limit on rows: all of one
person's windows go in the same batch, and every matching record comes back.
Smaller batches mean more, shorter queries and the same result:

```{r batches}
followup_small <- collect(followup_plan, batch_size = 100L)
nrow(followup_small)
setequal(paste(followup_small$entry_id, followup_small$tran_id),
         paste(followup$entry_id, followup$tran_id))

attr(followup_small, "window_report")
```

Here `r nrow(attr(followup_small, "window_report")$batches)` batches return the
same `r nrow(followup_small)` records, for the same entries, as one batch did.

Every collected result carries this report. `matched_entries` and
`unmatched_entries` count the entries with and without records: here the
`r sum(readmit$readmitted)` readmitted entries and the
`r sum(!readmit$readmitted)` others. `batches` shows each batch's people,
entries and matching records. `complete` is always `TRUE` on a result you get
back, because a failed batch stops with an error instead of returning part of
the result.

If a batch's query grows too large, `collect()` stops and asks for a smaller
`batch_size`. Batches keep queries short, but every returned record still ends
up in R's memory, so select the columns you need before you plan.

## Several entries per person

Here each person has one entry. If you keep several entries per person, such as
every appendicitis admission, give each its own `entry_id`. Their windows may
then overlap, and a record inside two windows comes back twice, once for each
entry. That is right when you count per entry. To count a person's admissions
instead, keep one of each with `distinct(pid, tran_id)`.

## In short

- `thip_window()` plans a round trip: each entry's person and window go to the
  database, and `collect()` brings back only the records inside, labelled with
  `entry_id`.
- A window is an index date and two day offsets. `"[)"` includes the first
  offset and excludes the second, so `c(1L, 31L)` from discharge is days 1 to
  30.
- `c(-365L, 0L)` from the admission date is the year before admission, without
  the entry admission.
- A window searches only the tables you stacked: set the edges from the data
  and check that windows fit inside them.
- Entries with no records are not in the result: start from `entries` and
  left-join.
- `thip_window()` keeps every match, so check for records repeated within an
  entry before you count.
- `start` and `end` give each window as two dates instead.
- `batch_size` counts people, not rows, and does not change the result;
  `attr(x, "window_report")` summarises the run.
